body.heading: The puzzle and its legend
paragraphs: A magic square arranges numbers so that every row, every column and both diagonals add to the same total — the magic constant. The most famous is the three-by-three using the numbers 1 to 9, where every line makes 15.

Chinese legend tells of the Lo Shu square, said to have been seen on the shell of a turtle emerging from the Luo River thousands of years ago. Whether or not the turtle existed, the square is real, and mathematicians have admired it ever since.

body.heading: Finding the heart of the square
paragraphs: Here is the key insight: the centre cell belongs to four different lines — a row, a column and both diagonals. The only number that can survive that much adding is 5, the middle number of 1 to 9. Put 5 in the centre and the puzzle is half solved.

Pairs that make 10 must sit opposite each other across the centre: 1 with 9, 2 with 8, 3 with 7, 4 with 6. One classic arrangement is 8-1-6 across the top, 3-5-7 through the middle, and 4-9-2 along the bottom. Check the diagonals: 8+5+2 and 6+5+4 both make 15.

body.heading: Try it: build and bend the square
paragraphs: Copy the classic square, then rotate it or flip it like a mirror. Every rotation and reflection still works, and those eight versions are the only solutions there are — the three-by-three magic square is, underneath, a single idea.

Now bend the rules: can you make a magic square using only even numbers, or the numbers 2 to 10? The constant changes, but the centre trick still guides you. Finding the new centre is your first move.

takeaway: In the three-by-three magic square, 5 holds the centre and every line makes 15 — one elegant idea with eight disguises.
